title: They Sold 16 Bodies to a Doctor. None of Them Died Naturally.
description: In 1828, two Irish labourers in Edinburgh discovered that a famous anatomy school would pay up to ten pounds for a fresh body, and never asked where it came from. This is the true story of Burke and Hare, the doctor who bought from them, and the law that finally ended the trade in human bodies.

scenes.say: In November 1827, two men carried a body through the dark streets of Edinburgh. They were taking it to a doctor. And that doctor was about to pay them more money than they could earn in two months of hard labour.

scenes.say: Within a year, the same two men would sell sixteen more bodies to the same doctor. And not one of those people died of natural causes.

scenes.say: Their names were William Burke and William Hare. This is the true story of how the greatest medical city in the world created a market for dead bodies, and how two poor men discovered that a human life could be sold for ten pounds.

scenes.say: In the 1820s, Edinburgh was famous for two things. Its dark, crowded old town. And its doctors. The University of Edinburgh had one of the best medical schools on Earth. Students came from all over Britain, from America, and from across Europe.

scenes.say: To become a surgeon, you had to understand the human body. And the only way to truly understand it was to open one up. Every student needed to see dissections with his own eyes, and the most popular teachers packed hundreds of students into a single room.

visuals.ai: a 16th century anatomical woodcut of a human figure
an old anatomical drawing

scenes.say: But there was a problem. By law, the only bodies doctors could legally dissect were those of executed criminals. And there were nowhere near enough executions. Some years, the medical schools of Scotland had only a handful of legal bodies, for hundreds of students.

scenes.say: Supply was tiny. Demand was enormous. And whenever that happens, a black market appears.

visuals.ai: a moonlit wet cobbled street at night, Victorian painting

scenes.say: The black market had a name. The resurrection men. Gangs who crept into graveyards at night, dug down to the head of a fresh coffin, broke it open, and pulled the body out with a rope. By morning, the grave looked untouched.

visuals.ai: two body snatchers digging up a grave at night, old engraving
an old Edinburgh graveyard with weathered tombstones

scenes.say: And here's the strange part. A dead body was not considered anyone's property. Taking the shroud or the coffin could be called theft. So the resurrection men were careful. They took the person, and left everything else behind.

visuals.ai: a plain wooden coffin in a dark room
two body snatchers digging up a grave at night, old engraving

scenes.say: Families were terrified. Rich ones paid for heavy iron cages called mortsafes, locked over the grave. Others hired watchmen, or took turns guarding their loved ones with guns. Watchtowers went up in graveyards all over Edinburgh. Some of them are still standing today.

visuals.ai: an iron cage over a grave, a mortsafe
an old Edinburgh graveyard with weathered tombstones
a small stone watchtower in a Scottish graveyard
an iron cage over a grave, a mortsafe
a moonlit wet cobbled street at night, Victorian painting
a small stone watchtower in a Scottish graveyard

scenes.say: As the graveyards got harder to rob, the price of a fresh body went up. By the late 1820s, an Edinburgh anatomist might pay seven to ten pounds for one. For a labourer earning a couple of shillings a day, that was months of wages. For a single night's work.

visuals.note: £10 = 200 shillings; a labourer earned roughly 2 shillings a day

scenes.say: William Burke was born in 1792 in Ulster, in the north of Ireland. He had been a soldier, a weaver, a baker's servant. Like thousands of poor Irishmen, he crossed to Scotland looking for work, and found it digging the new Union Canal outside Edinburgh.

visuals.ai: a 1828 sketch portrait of William Burke
a canal in the Scottish countryside
a canal in the Scottish countryside

scenes.say: William Hare was also Irish, and also a labourer. Almost nothing is known about his early life. Even his age is uncertain. What we do know is that he ended up in Edinburgh, living with a woman named Margaret Laird, who ran a cheap lodging house in a narrow alley called Tanner's Close, in the West Port.

visuals.ai: a 1828 sketch portrait of William Hare
a narrow old street in the West Port, Edinburgh
a dark narrow close in old Edinburgh, 19th century photograph
a dark stone alley in old Edinburgh
a narrow old street in the West Port, Edinburgh

scenes.say: In 1827, Burke and his partner, Helen McDougal, moved into that lodging house. The two Williams became friends. Drinking partners. And very soon, business partners.

visuals.ai: a dark stone alley in old Edinburgh
a lively Scottish tavern scene, 1820s painting
a Highland whisky still in a dark hut, painting

scenes.say: In November 1827, one of Hare's lodgers, an old army pensioner named Donald, died of illness in the house. He owed Hare four pounds in rent. Hare was furious. The old man had died owing him money.

visuals.ai: a poor 1820s room with a straw bed, painting
a dark narrow close in old Edinburgh, 19th century photograph

scenes.say: And then someone had an idea. Before the coffin was nailed shut, they lifted Donald out, filled the coffin with tree bark, and let it be buried. The mourners never knew the difference.

visuals.ai: a plain wooden coffin in a dark room
an old Edinburgh graveyard with weathered tombstones

scenes.say: That night, they asked a medical student where they could sell a body. He sent them to number ten Surgeons' Square, to the anatomy school of Doctor Robert Knox.

scenes.say: Knox was the most popular anatomy teacher in Edinburgh. Brilliant, arrogant, and always short of bodies. His assistants looked at Donald and paid seven pounds and ten shillings. And as the two men left, they were told the school would be glad to see them again, whenever they had another one to sell.

visuals.ai: a portrait of the anatomist Dr Robert Knox, 1820s

search: The Four Stages of Cruelty Hogarth
visuals.ai: an 18th century engraving of a public dissection
Surgeons' Square in Edinburgh, 19th century engraving

scenes.say: Knox had been an army surgeon, treating soldiers wounded at the Battle of Waterloo. Now, in his thirties, he ran his own school, and he had a reputation for always having bodies to show his students when other teachers did not. That reputation was money. Students paid fees to attend, and the more bodies he had, the more students came.

visuals.ai: a portrait of the anatomist Dr Robert Knox, 1820s

scenes.say: Seven pounds, ten shillings. Almost double the rent the old man had owed. And it took one night.

visuals.ai: a moonlit wet cobbled street at night, Victorian painting

scenes.say: The problem was, people don't die on schedule. Burke and Hare could have waited for the next lodger to die. Instead, early in 1828, they decided not to wait.

visuals.ai: a dark narrow close in old Edinburgh, 19th century photograph

scenes.say: Their first victim was a lodger called Joseph, a miller who had fallen sick with a fever. They were worried a fever in the house would scare away the other lodgers. So they gave him whisky until he could barely move, and then they smothered him.

visuals.ai: a poor 1820s room with a straw bed, painting
a Highland whisky still in a dark hut, painting
a dark stone alley in old Edinburgh

scenes.say: This became their method. Lure someone in, often a poor stranger with no family nearby. Get them drunk. Then Burke would press down on the chest while the nose and mouth were covered. It left almost no marks. To a doctor, it looked like someone who had simply died.

visuals.ai: Scottish working men drinking in an inn, painting
a Highland whisky still in a dark hut, painting
antique surgical instruments in a wooden case

scenes.say: The method became so infamous that it gave the English language a new word. To burke someone means to smother them, or to quietly hush something up. The word is still in the dictionary today.

visuals.ai: a 1828 sketch portrait of William Burke

scenes.say: And Knox kept paying. Ten pounds in winter. Eight in summer, because bodies spoiled faster in the heat. Nobody asked how two labourers kept finding such fresh bodies, with no sign of disease, and no grave dirt on them.

visuals.ai: a portrait of the anatomist Dr Robert Knox, 1820s
Surgeons' Square in Edinburgh, 19th century engraving

scenes.say: Over the next ten months, the killings followed a pattern. An old woman named Abigail Simpson, who had come into town to collect a small pension. A woman from England. A poor cinder gatherer known as Effy. A drunk woman being led away by the police, whom Burke politely offered to take home.

visuals.ai: the Grassmarket in Edinburgh, 19th century
a dark narrow close in old Edinburgh, 19th century photograph

search: Atkinson Grimshaw Liverpool Quay by Moonlight
visuals.ai: a dark moonlit Victorian street, painting

scenes.say: Most victims were people the city didn't see. The poor, the old, the homeless, strangers passing through. People who could disappear without anyone reporting them missing. That was the business model. Choose the people nobody would look for.

visuals.ai: the crowded old town of Edinburgh in the 1820s, tall dark stone houses
a dark stone alley in old Edinburgh
a grim Victorian workhouse, engraving

scenes.say: One victim was an old woman travelling with her grandson, a deaf boy of about twelve. Both were killed. Burke later said that this was the murder that haunted him most.

visuals.ai: the Grassmarket in Edinburgh, 19th century
a 1828 sketch portrait of William Burke

scenes.say: By the end, there were sixteen victims. Sixteen people. And each one was carried through the streets in a box or a sack, and sold across a table at Surgeons' Square.

visuals.ai: a moonlit wet cobbled street at night, Victorian painting
Surgeons' Square in Edinburgh, 19th century engraving

scenes.say: But then they made a mistake. They started killing people who were known. In April 1828, Burke met two young women in a pub. One of them was Mary Paterson, eighteen years old. She went back with him, and she never came out.

visuals.ai: a lively Scottish tavern scene, 1820s painting
an 1820s sketch of a young Scottish woman
visuals.caption: Mary Paterson, 18

scenes.say: When her body was laid out at Knox's school, some of the students recognised her. One even said he had seen her alive just days before. Questions were asked. Burke claimed she had drunk herself to death. And the questions stopped.

search: The Four Stages of Cruelty Hogarth
visuals.ai: an 18th century engraving of a public dissection
a portrait of the anatomist Dr Robert Knox, 1820s

scenes.say: According to some accounts, Knox was so struck by her body that he kept it preserved in a barrel of whisky for three months, and had his students draw it.

visuals.ai: a Highland whisky still in a dark hut, painting
an old anatomical drawing

scenes.say: Then came James Wilson. Everyone in Edinburgh knew him as Daft Jamie, a gentle eighteen year old with a disability who wandered the streets barefoot, telling riddles. He was one of the most recognisable people in the city.

visuals.ai: an 1820s sketch of a barefoot young man in Edinburgh
visuals.caption: James Wilson, 'Daft Jamie'

visuals.ai: the crowded old town of Edinburgh in the 1820s, tall dark stone houses
the Grassmarket in Edinburgh, 19th century
an 1820s sketch of a barefoot young man in Edinburgh

scenes.say: Jamie fought back. It took both men to kill him. And when his body arrived on Knox's table, the students knew him at once. According to later accounts, Knox insisted it was not Jamie, and began the dissection early, starting with the face.

visuals.ai: a dark stone alley in old Edinburgh

search: The Four Stages of Cruelty Hogarth
visuals.ai: an 18th century engraving of a public dissection
a portrait of the anatomist Dr Robert Knox, 1820s

scenes.say: Think about that. A doctor who must have known something was very wrong, and chose to say nothing. Because the bodies were fresh, and the price was right.

visuals.ai: a portrait of the anatomist Dr Robert Knox, 1820s
the columned front of Surgeons' Hall in Edinburgh

scenes.say: The end began on Halloween, 1828. Burke met a small Irish woman named Margaret Docherty in a shop, and found out she came from the same part of Ireland as him. He invited her home for a drink, to celebrate.

visuals.ai: a narrow old street in the West Port, Edinburgh
Scottish working men drinking in an inn, painting

scenes.say: There was a problem. Burke had lodgers of his own, a couple called James and Ann Gray. That night, he paid them to sleep somewhere else. The next morning, the old woman was gone, and Burke wouldn't let anyone near a pile of straw at the foot of the bed.

visuals.ai: a poor 1820s room with a straw bed, painting

search: Atkinson Grimshaw Liverpool Quay by Moonlight
visuals.ai: a dark moonlit Victorian street, painting
a poor 1820s room with a straw bed, painting

scenes.say: When Burke stepped out, Ann Gray looked under the straw.

visuals.ai: a poor 1820s room with a straw bed, painting

scenes.say: On their way to the police, the Grays were stopped by Helen McDougal. She begged them to keep quiet, and offered them ten pounds a week. A fortune. They refused. And they went to the police anyway.

visuals.ai: a dark narrow close in old Edinburgh, 19th century photograph

visuals.label: Offered every week to stay silent

visuals.ai: the crowded old town of Edinburgh in the 1820s, tall dark stone houses

scenes.say: By the time the police searched the house, the body was gone. But they followed the trail to Knox's school. And there, packed in a tea chest, they found her.

visuals.ai: a moonlit wet cobbled street at night, Victorian painting
Surgeons' Square in Edinburgh, 19th century engraving
an old wooden tea chest

scenes.say: Now the authorities had a serious problem. They had a body. They had suspects. But they had almost no proof of murder. The doctors who examined Margaret Docherty could not say for certain how she died. That was the whole point of the method.

visuals.ai: the great hall of Parliament House, Edinburgh's old court
antique surgical instruments in a wooden case

scenes.say: So the Lord Advocate made a deal. One of the killers could go free, if he testified against the other. Hare took the deal. He turned King's evidence, and stood up in court against his friend.

visuals.ai: the great hall of Parliament House, Edinburgh's old court
a 1828 sketch portrait of William Hare
visuals.caption: William Hare

visuals.ai: a 1828 sketch portrait of William Burke

scenes.say: The trial began on Christmas Eve, 1828. It went on through the night and into Christmas morning. Burke was found guilty of murdering Margaret Docherty. Helen McDougal got a verdict that only exists in Scotland. Not proven. She walked out of court, free.

visuals.ai: an 1828 courtroom sketch
the great hall of Parliament House, Edinburgh's old court
an 1828 courtroom sketch

scenes.say: Burke was sentenced to hang. And then, in a twist the whole city noticed, his body was to be publicly dissected. The man who sold bodies to the anatomists would end up on their table.

search: The Four Stages of Cruelty Hogarth
visuals.ai: an 18th century engraving of a public dissection

search: Old College University of Edinburgh engraving
visuals.ai: the University of Edinburgh Old College, 19th century engraving

scenes.say: While he waited to die, Burke gave a full confession. He went through the murders one by one, and a newspaper printed his story. People across Britain read every word. It's the main reason we know so much about what happened inside that lodging house.

visuals.ai: a 1828 sketch portrait of William Burke
the crowded old town of Edinburgh in the 1820s, tall dark stone houses

scenes.say: On the twenty eighth of January, 1829, Burke was hanged in the Lawnmarket, in front of a crowd of around twenty five thousand people. People paid for windows with a view. When he dropped, the crowd cheered.

visuals.ai: the Lawnmarket street in Edinburgh, 19th century
a huge crowd at a public execution in 1829, engraving
a crowd in an old city square, engraving

scenes.say: The next day, the professor of anatomy, Alexander Monro, dissected him in front of a packed lecture hall. Students rioted outside, trying to get in. Afterwards, tens of thousands of people filed past what was left of him.

visuals.ai: a portrait of an Edinburgh anatomy professor, 1820s

search: Old College University of Edinburgh engraving
visuals.ai: the University of Edinburgh Old College, 19th century engraving

search: The Four Stages of Cruelty Hogarth
visuals.ai: an 18th century engraving of a public dissection
a crowd in an old city square, engraving

scenes.say: Monro dipped his quill in Burke's blood and wrote a note. That note still survives.

visuals.text: This is written with the blood of Wm Burke, who was hanged at Edinburgh. This blood was taken from his head.

visuals.ai: a portrait of an Edinburgh anatomy professor, 1820s

scenes.say: And here's the darkest twist of all. Burke's skeleton is still on display today, at the University of Edinburgh's Anatomical Museum. And a small pocketbook, made from his tanned skin, is kept at Surgeons' Hall Museums. He became exactly what he sold.

visuals.ai: a human skeleton in a museum case
a plaster death mask of a man
the columned front of Surgeons' Hall in Edinburgh
a small old brown leather pocketbook

scenes.say: And the others? Hare was released in February 1829. Crowds recognised him and tried to attack him. He was smuggled out of the city, last seen heading south toward England, and then he vanished. Nobody knows where he went, or how he died.

visuals.ai: a 1828 sketch portrait of William Hare

search: Atkinson Grimshaw Liverpool Quay by Moonlight
visuals.ai: a dark moonlit Victorian street, painting

scenes.say: Helen McDougal and Margaret Laird were also attacked by angry crowds, and fled. Their fates are unknown too.

visuals.ai: a crowd in an old city square, engraving

scenes.say: And Doctor Knox was never charged with anything. A committee decided he had not known about the murders, but criticised how carelessly he bought bodies. Crowds burned his effigy and smashed his windows. His career in Edinburgh slowly collapsed, and he spent his final years in London, far from the fame he once had.

visuals.ai: a portrait of the anatomist Dr Robert Knox, 1820s
a view over 1820s Edinburgh with the castle, painting
a London street around 1830, painting
a portrait of the anatomist Dr Robert Knox, 1820s

scenes.say: The children of Edinburgh even made up a skipping rhyme about it.

visuals.text: Burke's the butcher, Hare's the thief, Knox the boy that buys the beef.

scenes.say: But the story didn't end with a hanging. Across Britain, people finally saw what the system had created. When you make something rare and valuable, someone will find a way to supply it. Even when the thing is a human body.

visuals.ai: the old Houses of Parliament in London around 1830, painting
grave robbers with lanterns in a churchyard, engraving

scenes.say: In 1831, a gang in London, soon nicknamed the London Burkers, murdered a young boy and tried to sell his body to the anatomy school at King's College. Britain had seen enough. A year later, Parliament passed the Anatomy Act. Medical schools could now receive unclaimed bodies from workhouses and hospitals, and anatomists needed a licence. The price of a body collapsed, and the murder market disappeared almost overnight.

visuals.ai: a London street around 1830, painting
the old Houses of Parliament in London around 1830, painting
a grim Victorian workhouse, engraving

scenes.say: But notice who paid the price again. The new law took the bodies of the poorest people, those who died in workhouses with no one to claim them. The poor were still the supply. Only now, it was legal.

visuals.ai: a grim Victorian workhouse, engraving

scenes.say: So what does a story from 1828 teach us about money? First. When a rule creates huge demand and tiny supply, it doesn't stop the demand. It creates a black market. And a black market always finds the weakest people.

visuals.ai: two body snatchers digging up a grave at night, old engraving
a dark stone alley in old Edinburgh

scenes.say: Second. Not asking is a business decision. Knox never killed anyone. But he made it profitable, and he chose not to ask the one question that would have stopped it.

visuals.ai: a portrait of the anatomist Dr Robert Knox, 1820s
Surgeons' Square in Edinburgh, 19th century engraving

scenes.say: And third. In every one of these deals, the people with the least power were the product. The old soldier. The woman with her pension. The boy. The girl from the pub. Sixteen lives, turned into ten pounds each.

visuals.ai: the Grassmarket in Edinburgh, 19th century
an 1820s sketch of a young Scottish woman

scenes.say: Altogether, Burke and Hare probably made something like a hundred and fifty pounds from all those lives. Burke paid with his own. Hare, who did the same things, walked away. And somewhere, nobody knows where, he lived out the rest of his life.

visuals.ai: a 1828 sketch portrait of William Burke
a 1828 sketch portrait of William Hare
